text_post: Don’t confuse the term “open source” with open to any and all attacks. It isn’t In fact, most open source software is FAR more secure than closed source because it’s open to wide scrutiny. Open source means that the human-readable source code is available to all to tinker with and change if they like. This means thousands of eyeb~~~~ are scrutinizing it looking for potential security holes in the final running (compiled) version. It also means that if a vulnerability is found, it gets fixed MUCH faster. Most open source vulnerabilities are in reality only *potential* security holes that were fixed before anyone could ever come up with an exploit. Closed source software relies entirely on the company that makes it finding and fixing vulnerabilities. Compare that to the army of volunteers in the open source world. If you’re concerned about security on your computers etc, I highly recommend considering switching to Linux. It’s basically impervious to viruses, and recent versions have damn near bulletproof security when connected to the internet depending on how you configure them.

text_post: And to be really clear, when I say that the code is open and available to tinker with, I don’t mean that YOUR software running on your system is open – it isn’t. It means that you have the source code and are able to build your own copy from scratch or make changes to it if you choose – but you can’t just change someone else’s running software.
